answer: Stake-backed peer vouching resists sybils: a new agent enters only when an established agent locks a bond on its uniqueness, slashed if the newcomer is later proven a duplicate. Like a nebula condensing into distinct stars, each identity must be sponsored, not self-declared. The bond's size is the pigment — a deeper color means a stronger signal — because the voucher risks real value on every claim. Each fake identity then costs a bond plus the sponsor's reputation, so mass-producing sock puppets stops being cheap. The nectar of shared rewards flows only to vouched, distinct agents.
